note: Researched jobs and the setup an experienced integrator would expect for each. Research estimates, not simulation results, except where a task links to a worked example.

tasks.title: Utility-scale solar module installation on trackers

subtasks.note: Use a vacuum frame and blow off dust before sealing.

subtasks.object: module onto the rail or torque-tube clamps
subtasks.note: One deployed system reports placement within plus or minus 1 mm.
Shared mid-clamps are torqued as the next module goes on.

tools: Vacuum frame, 4 to 6 cups, per-cup vacuum, blow-off
Nut runner on a short offset axis

tasks.why: The module must never sit unsecured in wind. A vacuum frame with an offset nut runner torques the shared clamp while the new module is still held, so one arm does what production systems do with two.

tasks.title: Asphalt shingle roofing: place and nail shingles

subtasks.note: Paired suction cups give a fallback when one lands on an edge.
A camera on the previous course checks exposure and offset.
Drive 4 to 6 nails while the shingle is still held.

tools: Suction cup array, single and paired cups
Coil nailers, 2 to 4, fixed along the nail line

tasks.why: A floppy shingle cannot be re-registered after release, so it must stay held at its course line while nailed. Nailers on the same head make that possible.

tasks.title: Interior wall and ceiling spray painting

subtasks.note: The crew does this and the robot avoids masked zones.

subtasks.object: wall and ceiling field in overlapping passes
subtasks.note: Constant standoff and overlap set coverage and film uniformity.
A camera inspects, then touch-up is by hand or a second pass.

tools: Airless spray gun with fan tip and standoff sensor

tasks.why: One nozzle on a lift-mounted arm covers walls and ceilings, and standoff and overlap control the result. A dual-nozzle bar only adds throughput. A roller wins only where overspray is unacceptable.

tasks.title: Ceiling drilling and anchor installation

subtasks.note: Use a total station or building model and avoid rebar.
Use dust extraction and depth sensing.
Hammer-set or torque-set, a step some deployed systems skip.

tools: Rotary hammer with dust shroud and depth stop

tasks.why: Drill every hole in reach, swap once, set every anchor, then move the base. Batching makes the swap almost free and covers anchor setting, where the remaining labour is.

tasks.title: Floor tile setting: spread adhesive, place and level tiles

subtasks.note: Production robots spread one lane at a time from an applicator on the mobile base.

subtasks.object: tile onto the bed at joint offset
subtasks.note: Vision sets the joint, so no plastic spacers are needed.
Vibrate or press until lippage to neighbours is under about 1 mm.

tools: Vacuum pad array, 4 to 6 cups, with vibration tamper

tasks.why: Spread one lane, swap once, then set it, so the swap stays cheap. The tamper sits inside the vacuum head because the tile must be vibrated into the bed.

tasks.title: Drywall hanging on walls and ceilings

subtasks.note: Use a vacuum frame and separate the top sheet.

subtasks.object: board against studs or ceiling grid
subtasks.note: It must stay held until the first screws are in.
Limit depth so heads dimple the paper without tearing it.

tools: Board vacuum frame, 4 to 6 foam cups, dual circuit
Autofeed screw spindle on a short linear axis

tasks.why: The board must stay flat against the framing while the first screws go in, and one arm cannot swap tools mid-hold. A spindle on the vacuum frame lets the arm hold and fasten in one pose.

tasks.title: Bricklaying: butter, lay and level bricks to the line

subtasks.note: Bed and head joints are buttered at a station before placing.

subtasks.object: brick to the line and level
subtasks.note: A camera corrects for how the brick sits in the gripper, with joints of about 10 mm.
This step stays with the mason in every deployed system.

tools: Parallel brick clamp, long flat padded jaws
Camera for brick offset in the jaws

tasks.why: A padded parallel clamp grips a rigid brick repeatably and leaves the bed and head faces free for mortar. Mortar comes from a fixed buttering station or a separate mortar robot, so the arm never changes tools.

tasks.title: Rebar tying at bar intersections

subtasks.note: A camera finds the crossings without pre-mapping in one deployed system.
The jaws must enclose both bars.
One tool cycle takes about a second.

tasks.why: The tie itself is a solved product, so the integrator buys a tying unit and only solves positioning. A gripper plus a wire twister would reinvent the tool.

tasks.title: Window and glass panel installation

subtasks.note: A vacuum frame picks from a tilted rack.

subtasks.object: unit into the frame on setting blocks
subtasks.note: Tilt and translate with clearance on every side and a force-limited set-down.

subtasks.object: unit while beads or clips are fixed
subtasks.note: Fixing stays with the glazier.

tools: Vacuum pad frame, 4 to 8 pads, dual circuit

tasks.why: Glazing robots on the market all use a multi-pad, dual-circuit vacuum frame, so the tool is solved. The engineering lies in the manipulator and the tilt-and-insert motion.

tasks.title: Floor layout marking from the building model

subtasks.note: A total station tracks a prism on the robot.
The robot avoids obstacles within edge clearance limits.
Inkjet ink is chosen for surface and temperature.

tasks.why: Layout involves no manipulation. The effector is a print head and the robot is the mobile base, so an arm adds nothing.

tasks.title: Concrete and clay block laying

subtasks.object: adhesive or mortar to the block bed
subtasks.note: An in-line applicator works before the gripper in one deployed system.
The heavy payload needs a slow, stiff trajectory.
A laser or camera checks the result.

tools: Servo clamp gripper, 300 to 400 mm flat jaws

tasks.why: The logic matches bricks but the units are heavier, so a strong clamp is the only tool. Adhesive goes on in-line before the gripper takes the block.

tasks.title: Offsite timber wall framing: place studs and nail plates

subtasks.object: stud between the plates at spacing
subtasks.note: The stud sits square to the plate.
Two nails go in each end while the stud is held square.
This is often done on a separate nailing bridge.

tools: Pneumatic framing nailer beside the jaws

tasks.why: The stud must stay square to the plate while it is nailed, and a nailer beside the gripper lets one arm place and fasten in one pose. Production lines often split this between a placing robot and a nailing bridge.

tasks.title: Vinyl or laminate plank flooring, click-lock installation

subtasks.note: A vacuum bar runs along the plank.

subtasks.object: plank into the previous row's groove
subtasks.note: Rotate about the long edge, push and lower so the short end folds down to lock.
The same tool gives a force-limited sideways push.

tools: Vacuum bar, 2 to 3 cups, on a force-torque sensing wrist

tasks.why: The arm's own motion closes the click joint by angling, pushing and dropping, then a sideways push finishes it. Force sensing matters more than special tooling.

tasks.title: Exterior facade spray painting from a lift

subtasks.note: Wash and clean the surface, which some robots also do.

subtasks.object: facade in fixed-size boxes from the lift
subtasks.note: One deployed system scans a box of about 50 sq ft, then sprays it, box by box.
Imaging checks quality and guides touch-up.

tools: Multi-nozzle spray bar on a 2-axis gantry

tasks.why: Large flat facades suit a wide spray bar moving in a raster better than an articulated arm. The lift supplies the reach.

tasks.title: Curtain wall bracket installation at the slab edge

subtasks.object: bracket position at the slab edge
subtasks.note: A total station gives the reference.

subtasks.object: anchor holes or scan the cast-in channel
subtasks.note: A hammer drill works near the edge.

subtasks.object: bracket with bolts torqued to spec
subtasks.note: Torque is logged for each bracket.

tools: Rotary hammer drill with dust shroud
Nut runner or pulse torque driver with bracket fingers

tasks.why: Drilling and fastening happen in sequence, so drill every hole in reach, swap once, then fasten. One deployed system uses this approach with two arms per base, so one arm holds while the other drives.

tasks.title: Overhead pipe and conduit installation on hangers

subtasks.note: Spin each rod in to depth.

subtasks.object: pipe or conduit into the hangers
subtasks.note: 3 m sticks need support at two points.
Close the clamp and torque the nuts.

tools: Parallel gripper with V-jaws sized to the pipe range

tasks.why: Rods go up first along a run, pipe is seated later and clamps come last, so one swap per run is enough. V-jaws centre round stock of different sizes, and one nut runner spins rods and tightens clamp nuts.

tasks.title: Wall tile setting, butter, press and align tiles

subtasks.note: A comb pass at a fixed station keeps adhesive fresh for each tile.

subtasks.object: tile onto the wall at joint offset
subtasks.note: Push and slide into the bed, then hold briefly so the tile does not slip.
A camera or laser checks against neighbours, with lippage under about 1 mm.

tools: Vacuum pad array, 4 cups, with force-controlled pressing plate

tasks.why: Wall tiles are small and light, so one vacuum head pressing with controlled force is enough. Buttering at a fixed station keeps the arm on one tool and stops adhesive skinning on the wall.

tasks.title: Drywall finishing, spray joint compound and sand

subtasks.object: joint compound on seams or full skim
subtasks.note: Level 4 covers seams, Level 5 covers the whole wall.

subtasks.object: dried compound to a flat finish
subtasks.note: Orbital sanding at steady contact force with dust extraction, as compound scratches easily.
This step is optional and uses the same spray tool.

tools: Random-orbit sander with vacuum shroud on force-controlled wrist

tasks.why: Hours of drying separate spraying and sanding, so one swap per pass costs nothing. The key choice is force control for sanding, which one deployed system gets from the arm's built-in force control.

tasks.title: Facade cladding and retrofit panel installation

subtasks.note: Drill and anchor across the whole bay first.
Lift the panel, then align it finely.
Use screws or clips.

tools: Vacuum pad frame for panel hanging
Drill driver for brackets and fixings

tasks.why: Brackets go on across a whole bay before any panel is hung, so the tool swap happens once per bay, not per panel. A crane or cable robot often takes the heavy lift, while the arm aligns and fastens.

tasks.title: Deck and roof fastener driving

subtasks.object: joist, purlin or high rib below
subtasks.note: Find it through the deck or insulation.

subtasks.object: screw with plate to depth or torque
subtasks.note: The fastener is the same every time.
Mark failures for rework.

tools: Autofeed screw spindle, strip or blow feed

tasks.why: Every fastener is identical, so an autofeed spindle on a carriage or gantry beats an arm picking screws one by one. No timber decking robot was found, but the same tool applies.

tasks.title: Shear stud and bracket welding on structural steel

subtasks.object: stud and ferrule into the gun
subtasks.note: Studs and ferrules come from bowl feeders.
Hold it perpendicular to the flange.
The arc lasts about a second, then bend test a sample.

tools: Stud welding gun with stud and ferrule feed

tasks.why: The gun picks and holds the stud and the feeders present studs and ferrules, so no gripper is needed. Bracket and column welds need a welding torch with a seam sensor instead.

tasks.title: Rebar placement on chairs at spacing

subtasks.note: This step is contact rich and the hardest to automate.
Support at several points stops long bars swinging.
Do this before tying.

tools: Spreader beam with 2 to 4 V-jaw parallel grippers

tasks.why: Long bars sag and swing, so gripping at several points keeps them straight. A lifting magnet suits black bar but likely loses hold on epoxy coated bar and cannot lift fibreglass bar, both used on bridge decks.

tasks.title: Caulking and sealant joints on facades and windows

subtasks.note: The deformable foam rod stays a crew task.
Angle the nozzle into the joint at a constant speed matched to flow.
Use a trailing shoe or spatula.

tasks.why: One pass can bead and tool the joint if a shoe trails the nozzle. The tracker keeps the nozzle centred on a joint that wanders, and backer rod stays with the crew.

tasks.title: Tile grouting: fill joints and wipe haze

subtasks.note: Use a rubber float or squeegee in diagonal passes.
Fill to depth, as compression matters, not only surface finish.
Use a damp sponge after initial set.

tools: Rubber float or squeegee head, compliant mount
Damp sponge pad or roller with water feed

tasks.why: The grout set time separates floating from wiping, so working zone by zone needs one tool swap per zone. A combined head adds weight for no gain.

tasks.title: Hardened concrete wall and ceiling grinding

subtasks.note: Use a laser scan or a straightedge.
A diamond cup wheel with a dust shroud works at steady contact force.
Rescan the surface.

tools: Diamond cup-wheel grinder with vacuum shroud

tasks.why: The job needs only one abrasive tool. The real engineering is in controlling contact force and capturing dust, so a compliant, force-controlled mount with a vacuum shroud fits.

tasks.title: Rigid insulation board installation, spray foam variant

subtasks.note: Apply dabs or a ribbon at a station.

subtasks.object: board in staggered bond, tight to neighbours
subtasks.note: Gaps cause thermal bridges.
Drill and set a dowel per area.

tools: Large low-vacuum foam pad or needle gripper
Drill with anchor and dowel driver

tasks.why: Boards go up course by course and anchors follow per area, so one tool swap per area is enough. Mineral wool is porous, so a needle gripper replaces the vacuum pad there.

tasks.title: Fresh concrete floor screeding and troweling

subtasks.note: Use a laser-referenced screed.
Float after the bleed water.
Make several power-trowel passes.

tools: Rotary trowel discs or blades on a mobile base

tasks.why: This is a machine task, not an arm task. The effector is the trowel rotor and the mobile base carries it.

tasks.title: Mixed item piece picking for order fulfilment

subtasks.object: one item from a cluttered mixed tote
subtasks.note: Boxes and blister packs are rigid, but polybags wrinkle and break suction seals.
A fixed scanner or scan tunnel usually reads it, and the robot only presents or drops the item.

subtasks.object: the item into the order tote or cubby
subtasks.note: No precise orientation is needed.

tasks.why: Suction is the usual default for single items, and one deployed system reported 97% first-pick success in fashion with one high-flow cup. Add fingers to the cup only for many books, granular bags or heavy items.

tasks.title: Two-piece shoebox picking

subtasks.object: the shoebox base and lid together
subtasks.note: The lid is loose, so a top suction pick lifts only the lid.

subtasks.object: the closed box without the lid sliding off
subtasks.note: Accelerations matter.

subtasks.object: the box into the sorter pocket
subtasks.note: The start pose may be vertical or horizontal.

tools: Long-stroke parallel jaw gripper with tall flat pads

tasks.why: Squeezing the box from two sides across the lid seam holds base and lid together, while suction on the top lifts only the lid. Two-piece boxes have long defeated standard vacuum and mechanical grippers.

tasks.title: Mixed-case depalletising

subtasks.object: the top-layer case from a mixed pallet
subtasks.note: Sizes are unknown, with shrink wrap and shifted stacks.

subtasks.object: the case without it peeling off
subtasks.note: Tall light cases peel off a vacuum tool under acceleration.

subtasks.object: the case on the outbound conveyor
subtasks.note: Business rules set the orientation.

tasks.why: Vacuum touches only the top face, so it works on any stack pattern and is the most common depalletising tool. Add side clamps only when tall, light cases peel off under acceleration.

tasks.title: Palletising cases and bags

subtasks.note: Items can be sealed corrugate, trays or bags.
Gaps and squareness matter for stability.
The sheet is thin and flat, so the same vacuum tool lifts it.

tasks.why: For sealed cases a vacuum tool is enough and also lifts tier sheets. Change tool by product: forks for bags and open trays, clamps for pails, and a combined vacuum and clamp head only for mixed-product cells.

tasks.title: Trailer and container unloading of floor-loaded cartons

subtasks.note: Cartons near the ceiling must be gripped from the front.
Deployed systems handle this.

tasks.why: Deployed production systems use suction alone. It grips the exposed front or top face, which is all a wall of cartons offers.

tasks.title: E-commerce packing: erect box, place items, close box

subtasks.note: Open the tube, then fold and lock the bottom flaps against a fixture.
The same vacuum tool picks the items.
A standard tape sealer then seals the box.

tools: Multi-cup suction gripper, individual cup control

tasks.why: One vacuum gripper does all three steps in a collaborative robot cell, folding flaps against fixed guides. At high volume a dedicated machine handles the boxes and the robot only places items.

tasks.title: Returns processing: unpack, identify, sort

subtasks.note: Opening the bag needs deformable handling, so leave it to a person or a dual-arm station.
Use a scan tunnel or present the item to a scanner.

tools: Multi-cup suction gripper, individual cup control

tasks.why: Once the item is out of the mailer, the job is pick, scan and sort, using the same suction tool as piece picking and a fixed scan tunnel. Opening mailers needs two arms and is outside a single-tool cell.

tasks.title: Parcel singulation, induction and scanning

subtasks.object: one parcel from a bulk pile
subtasks.note: Avoid double picks.
A six-sided tunnel downstream does the scanning.

subtasks.object: non-conveyable parcels to an exception path

tools: Multi-cup suction gripper, individual cup control

tasks.why: Deployed systems use multi-cup suction with control of each cup, so one tool holds a small mailer or a large box. Scanning belongs to a fixed tunnel, not the tool.

tasks.title: Print-and-apply labelling of cases and pallets

subtasks.object: printed label from the peel plate
subtasks.note: A vacuum pad holds the label.

subtasks.object: label to the case or pallet face
subtasks.note: The labelling standard asks for 400 to 800 mm above the pallet base, at least 50 mm from a vertical edge, ideally on two sides.
A scanner sits on the tool.

tasks.why: The printer stays fixed and the robot carries only a light vacuum pad and scanner. Nothing else is needed.

tasks.title: Case-to-tote decanting

subtasks.note: This is usually done by a fixed case-opening machine.

tasks.why: The cutting stays in a fixed opener, so the robot only lifts inner packs, which suction does best. A knife on the robot would add a tool change per case for no gain.

tasks.title: Stowing items into fabric pod cubbies

subtasks.note: One deployed system uses a second arm with a hook.
A force-limited spatula blade does this.
Paddles with built-in belts slide it in.

tasks.why: This follows one deployed system: the stow tool combines plates, belts and a spatula, and a second arm holds the band. Use it only for front-access cubbies, as open-top totes need none of it.

tasks.title: Beverage cooler restocking from behind the shelf

subtasks.object: bottle or can from stock case
subtasks.note: This covers cans of all sizes and PET bottles up to 2 L.
The arm is mounted on a rail.
The robot picks the lane by what is running short.

tasks.why: One simple gripper covers every can and PET bottle in the cooler. One deployed robot uses a clip-like hand, and no second tool is needed.

tasks.title: Grocery shelf restocking and facing for boxes and cans

subtasks.object: product from tightly packed shipping case
subtasks.note: Use side grasps on boxes and cans.

subtasks.object: product in a tight row on the shelf
subtasks.note: Humans leave gaps of about 3 mm.
This is a non-prehensile push.

tools: Parallel jaw gripper with slim fingers

tasks.why: Slim parallel fingers grasp boxes and cans, and the closed fingers or palm push rows forward. A research system using one reached over 98% object-level success, with spacing, not tool type, the gap to humans.

tasks.title: Online grocery picking and bagging

subtasks.note: Items vary widely in weight, shape and fragility.
Order and density matter.

subtasks.object: items the tool cannot handle to a person
subtasks.note: Watermelons are one example.

tasks.why: One operator reports a small cup packs about 40% of its groceries and expects more only by adding a parallel gripper, soft attachments and a bottle tool. Tool change pays off because each extra tool unlocks a large volume class.

tasks.title: Garment handling: pick, hang, fold and bag

subtasks.object: polybagged or loose garment from a bin
subtasks.note: Use suction for polybags and a pinch grip for loose cloth.
The garment is deformable and outside rigid-body scope.
The garment is deformable.

tasks.why: In logistics most apparel is polybagged and picked by suction. Loose garments need a pinch gripper and cloth simulation, and hanging and folding are outside rigid-body scope.

tasks.title: Kitting parts into trays

subtasks.object: a part from a bin or shelf box
subtasks.note: Parts include bolts, brackets, caps and bearings.

subtasks.object: the part for its tray nest
subtasks.note: Orientation decides whether the part can be grasped.

subtasks.object: the part into the tray nest
subtasks.note: The kit sequence can be chosen to group parts by tool.

tasks.why: A two-finger gripper grasped more part types, though vacuum was faster where both worked in one published test. Use a tool change only if flat, light parts dominate, and sequence the kit to change tools once.

tasks.title: CNC machine tending: door, vise or chuck, load and unload

subtasks.note: The door is often automatic, but the arm can push or pull it.

subtasks.object: finished part for raw blank in vise or chuck
subtasks.note: Unload and then load in one visit.
This is done with an I/O signal.

tasks.why: A dual gripper unloads and loads in one visit, and one supplier reports a cycle cut from 27 s to 15 s. The same jaws push or pull the door, and the machine works its own vise or chuck.

tasks.title: Screw driving in assembly

subtasks.object: the cover or part onto the base in the fixture
subtasks.note: Skip this step if operators load the fixtures.
The tool holds the screw on the bit.
Repeat for each hole.

tasks.why: If people load the fixture, the screwdriver alone is enough. If the robot also places the part, each cycle alternates place and drive, so a compact gripper beside the driver beats a tool change per part.

tasks.title: Snap-fit clip insertion

subtasks.object: the clip over its tower or hole

subtasks.note: Force rises then drops at the snap.

tasks.why: At volume, a feeder-fed inserter avoids picking each clip. For low volume or several clip types, a parallel jaw with part-shaped fingers and a wrist force-torque sensor to detect the snap is more flexible.

tasks.title: Press-fit of bushings and bearings

subtasks.object: the housing into the press nest
the bushing or bearing onto the press tooling
subtasks.note: Orientation matters.
The press monitors force and travel.

tasks.why: Integrators let a servo press make the fit and use the robot to load it, with a dual gripper carrying housing and bushing together. The robot presses only light fits itself, using a parallel jaw and force-guided search.

tasks.title: Cable connector insertion for wire harnesses

subtasks.object: the connector housing at its grip ribs
subtasks.note: The hanging cable pulls on the connector.

subtasks.object: the connector into the socket with a force-guided search
subtasks.note: Position noise of plus or minus 2 mm is typical.

subtasks.object: the connector to confirm the latch

tools: Parallel jaw gripper with form-fit fingers

tasks.why: Form-fit fingers on a standard parallel gripper hold the connector rigidly, and the wrist force-torque sensor handles the search and latch check. A tool change is needed only when the next step uses a different fastener, such as a clip gun.

tasks.title: Deburring machined or cast parts

subtasks.object: part from a fixture or conveyor
part edges to a compliant spindle along a path
subtasks.note: Keep the pressure constant.

tools: Parallel jaw gripper with part-shaped jaws

tasks.why: For parts the arm can lift, integrators fix the compliant spindle and move the part, so a smaller arm can work with a bigger spindle. Mount the spindle on the robot only for parts too big to carry.

tasks.title: Sanding and polishing surfaces

subtasks.note: Use a 3D camera.

subtasks.object: surface at constant contact force along a coverage path

subtasks.note: Use a station, not a second tool.

tools: Orbital sander on an active compliant flange

tasks.why: The active flange holds contact force while the arm moves fast. One published test found it beat arm-based force control on quick orientation changes. Discs change at a station, so one tool is enough.

tasks.title: Quality inspection with part flipping

subtasks.object: face A of the part to the camera

subtasks.note: Use a flip station, a hand-off or an in-hand move.

subtasks.object: part to the OK or NG bin

tasks.why: One gripper and a passive V-nest do the job: set the part down and regrip it from the other side. One deployed system used a suction cup for flat machined parts. No tool change is needed within one part family.

tasks.title: Injection moulding part removal and degating

subtasks.object: part and runner from the open mould
subtasks.note: Use vacuum on the part and pliers on the runner.
Use a fixed nipper station or a knife on the tool.

subtasks.object: part on the conveyor and runner in the granulator

tasks.why: Cups for the part and pliers for the runner on one frame clear the mould in one stroke. Cutting at a fixed nipper station avoids adding knife mass inside the mould.

tasks.title: Sorting laser-cut parts from the skeleton

subtasks.object: cut part out of the skeleton
subtasks.note: A small wiggle may be needed to free micro-joints.

subtasks.object: part on its pallet by part number

subtasks.note: A fork system often does this, not the robot.

tasks.why: Magnets grip thick steel best, while aluminium and stainless need vacuum. Mixed-material shops change tools by job. A steel-only shop needs only the magnet.

tasks.title: Press brake tending

subtasks.object: blank from the stack and square it
subtasks.note: Check for double sheets and use a centring table.

subtasks.object: blank against the backgauge through the bend
subtasks.note: Follow the flange as it rises.

subtasks.object: part between bends and stack it
subtasks.note: Use a regrip station.

tools: Parallel jaw gripper with pivoting jaws

tasks.why: Vacuum takes blanks off the stack and jaws hold the edge as the flange swings up. Production machines combine both in one gripper with a fixed regrip station. Add a tool changer only for very different part families.

tasks.title: Battery module cell stacking

subtasks.object: one or a row of cells from the tray
subtasks.note: Cells may be prismatic, cylindrical or pouch.
Alternate the polarity and add spacers.

subtasks.object: end plates and compress the stack

tasks.why: A high-force, long-stroke parallel gripper with in-place detection is standard for prismatic cells, and it also places spacers and end plates. For densely packed round cells, use a magnetic top pick instead.

tasks.title: PCB test fixture loading and sorting

subtasks.object: PCB or panel from the magazine or tray
subtasks.note: Grip by the edge and keep it ESD-safe.

subtasks.object: board onto the fixture pins and close the lid
tested board to the pass or fail magazine

tasks.why: Wide-stroke edge fingers cover many board sizes without a change, which is why one manufacturer chose this gripper. The gripper can also push the lid closed.

tasks.title: Through-hole and odd-form component insertion

subtasks.object: component by its body or leads

subtasks.note: Tolerance is under a millimetre.
A machine does this under the board.

tasks.why: Odd-form parts differ too much for one gripper, so dedicated machines change heads by component class. Group insertions by tool to keep changes few.

tasks.title: Bottle capping with screw caps

subtasks.note: Find the thread start.

tasks.why: A gripper that holds the cap, plus wrist rotation with a torque limit, is enough. The arm's own torque sensing sets the tightness.

tasks.title: Open doors and drawers

subtasks.note: Turn or press as the latch needs.
Swing the door or slide the drawer.

tasks.why: One parallel gripper handles levers, knobs and drawer pulls, and one legged robot opens doors with a built-in single-axis gripper. A hook is cheaper and more forgiving if the job is only drawers and pull handles.

tasks.title: Load dish racks in a commercial dish room

subtasks.object: plate, bowl or cup from the bus tub or stack
ware upright into a peg rack
loaded rack into the dish machine

tasks.why: One deployed system settled on one gripper body with swappable fingers, since greasy plates, cups on their side and cutlery bunches each need different fingers. Fingers are cheap wear parts, and a fixed set would miss cutlery.

tasks.title: Deliver amenities to a hotel room by lift and door

subtasks.note: Exit at the right floor.
Present the item to the guest.

tools: Compliant fingertip button pusher with card holder

tasks.why: Every contact is a press or a tap, and the guest takes the item from a drawer. A rigid finger with a compliant tip presses buttons, knocks and taps a card, so no gripper is needed, as in one deployed system.

tasks.title: Move microplates between instruments

subtasks.object: plate into reader or incubator nest
subtasks.note: Seat it in the right orientation.

tools: Servo parallel gripper with plate paddles

tasks.why: Two force-controlled paddles grip the plate skirt and self-centre on the standard footprint, so one tool handles plates, lids and tip racks. Suction would need a second cup set to de-lid and cannot seal on foil-sealed or lidless plates.

tasks.title: Transfer and pack eggs

subtasks.object: a full row or tray of eggs
eggs into hatcher baskets or cartons

subtasks.note: Destack and restack them.

tools: Suction cup array at egg pitch

tasks.why: A cup array lifts a whole tray of eggs without squeezing the shells. A tray clamp on the same head lets one robot also handle trays. Drop the clamp if trays move on conveyors.

tasks.title: Trip and rack out a switchgear circuit breaker

subtasks.note: This opens the breaker.
Turn until the breaker reaches the disconnected position.

tools: Parallel gripper for trip button and tool placing

tasks.why: Racking takes dozens of turns at real torque, which an arm wrist should not do. The gripper presses the trip and places a motorised socket that does the turning. A dedicated remote racking device is cheaper when no mobile robot is needed.

tasks.title: Restock and face beverage coolers

subtasks.object: bottle or can from back stock
item into the correct shelf lane

subtasks.note: This faces the lane.

tools: Parallel gripper with concave bottle and can fingers

tasks.why: Bottles and cans are rigid cylinders in fixed lanes. One gripper picks them and, when closed, pushes lanes forward to face them, and one deployed system uses a single hand for every beverage shape.

tasks.title: Restock hospital supplies

subtasks.object: items from central-store bins into a tote

tools: Adaptive two-finger gripper, 85 mm stroke class

tasks.why: Supplies mix boxes, bottles and soft pouches. Adaptive fingers conform to all three and can also pull drawer handles, as in one deployed hospital robot.

tasks.title: Load a dishwasher

subtasks.note: Open the door and pull out the rack.
Push the rack in and close the door.

tools: Adaptive two-finger gripper, wide stroke, rubber pads

tasks.why: One adaptive gripper takes plates by the rim, bowls and glasses by the body, and the rack by its front edge. Learned policies already stack bowls with a parallel jaw, and hands are not needed for a tidy counter.

tasks.title: Harvest strawberries by cutting and gripping the stem

tools: Blade on the same actuator, cut-and-hold head

tasks.why: Gripping and cutting the stem in one closing stroke never squeezes the fruit and needs one actuator. In published lab tests, a 10 N stem grip held a 50 g berry under fast motion.

tasks.title: Decap and recap sample tubes

subtasks.object: tube upright in a rack or clamp

subtasks.note: Unscrew the cap and lift it.
Tighten to a set torque.

tools: Rotary parallel gripper with V-groove cap jaws

tasks.why: Decapping is a twist with the tube held still, so a rack or clamp holds the tube and one gripper that grips and spins endlessly twists, lifts and replaces the cap. For full standard racks a dedicated multi-way decapper is better than any arm.

tasks.title: Store and pick medicine packs

subtasks.object: incoming pack from the input belt

subtasks.note: Drop them into the output chute.

tools: Parallel jaw with long flat fingers

tasks.why: Packs are rigid boxes stored tightly, so thin flat fingers slide in beside a pack and a pusher ejects it. Suction works on an exposed face but handles only one face per pick.

tasks.title: Harvest tree fruit such as apples

subtasks.note: Convey or drop it into the bin.

tools: Soft bellows suction cup with vacuum

tasks.why: Most leading apple picking systems use suction, as it attaches despite position error and keeps fingers out of the canopy. Detachment is a wrist twist and pull.

tasks.title: Turn valves during plant operator rounds

subtasks.note: A quarter turn or several turns.

tasks.why: Deployed plant robots turn valves with their standard gripper, provided the wrist delivers the breakaway torque. A dedicated handwheel driver only pays off for stiff multi-turn wheels.

tasks.title: Space potted plants in a greenhouse or nursery

subtasks.object: pot to the next pattern point

tools: Wide-stroke two-jaw clamp gripper for pot rim or body

tasks.why: Pots are rigid cylinders in a known size range, so one clamp handles them, while suction fails on ribbed, dusty pots. For more throughput, repeat the same gripper on a multi-pot head.

tasks.title: Empty trash bins

subtasks.object: bin into the cart or truck hopper

tools: Wide-stroke clamp gripper for the bin body

tasks.why: Tipping a rigid bin is a clamp, lift and rotate, as side-loader arms already do for standard carts. Indoors the same clamp works if bins are standardised. Replacing liners needs cloth handling and stays manual.

tasks.title: Pick and place baked goods

subtasks.object: items into a slug for wrapping

tasks.why: Buns and pastries are soft, crumbly and porous, so suction leaks and pulls crumbs, while soft fingers cradle them. For flat, sealed items such as cookies, use a vacuum cup instead. Pick one tool per product family.

tasks.title: Run a fry station

subtasks.note: Grip the basket by its handle.
Shake the basket after lifting.
Hang the basket back afterwards.

tasks.why: Every step moves one rigid basket by its handle, and filling and dumping use dispensers and tilting. A handle-matched jaw is the cheapest secure grip near hot oil.

tasks.title: Clear a table
tasks.why: Items are rigid and sit on a flat table. The best published table-bussing results use a parallel jaw.

tasks.title: Pack produce into trays

subtasks.note: Avoid bruising.

tasks.why: Apples, tomatoes and citrus have sealable skins, and a bellows cup tolerates position error while the wrist turns the fruit stem up. Switch to soft fingers for fuzzy or irregular produce such as kiwi, peppers or bunches.

tasks.title: Load pipette-tip racks onto a liquid handler

subtasks.object: full tip rack in its deck slot

subtasks.note: The pipette head does this, not the gripper.

tools: Servo parallel gripper with plate paddles

tasks.why: Tip racks share the standard plate footprint, so the same plate gripper moves them with no extra tool. The pipette head makes the tip press fit itself, so the gripper only handles racks.

tasks.title: Sort sample tubes into racks

tools: Narrow parallel gripper, long V-groove tube fingers

tasks.why: Tubes are rigid cylinders in a few sizes in dense racks. Narrow fingers reach between neighbours and wrist rotation spins the tube for the barcode read, while suction fails on decapped and push-cap tubes.

tasks.title: Transplant seedlings from plug trays

subtasks.note: Pusher pins push it up from below.

subtasks.object: plug in destination cell or pot

tasks.why: Production transplanters grip the root plug after pins push it up. In one published test a two-finger gripper beat a needle gripper, 95% against 81.75%, as needles shatter loose plugs, so use fingers for loose-plug crops.

tasks.title: Clean commercial restrooms

subtasks.object: stall door and seat or lid

subtasks.note: Scrub as well if needed.
Vacuum or dry the floor and pick up trash.

tools: Parallel gripper for doors, seats and trash

tasks.why: Lids and doors need a grip and disinfection is a spray. One deployed touchless spray system avoids brushes but does not scrub under the rim, so add a brush only if inspections demand it.

tasks.title: Press lift buttons and building controls

subtasks.note: Tap the badge on the reader.

tasks.why: Buttons need a precise press with limited force, not a grasp. Research prototypes show even a simple arm with a pusher tip does the job.

tasks.title: Make coffee and drinks

subtasks.note: This covers the portafilter, levers and buttons.
Pour it or pass it over.

tasks.why: The liquids stay inside the machines, and the arm only moves cups, a portafilter or a pitcher and presses levers. One parallel gripper does all of this, and a hand only pays off for latte-art pours.

tasks.title: Sort surgical instruments into sterilisation trays
tasks.why: Instruments are thin, hinged, shiny and tangled. A magnet grips any ferromagnetic instrument without precise finger placement, as one research cell chose, though non-magnetic instruments would likely need fingers.

tasks.title: Handle blister cards and unit doses

subtasks.object: items into carton or unit-dose bag

tools: Vacuum cup array, food and drug grade silicone cups

tasks.why: The flat foil side of a blister seals well, and thin cards slip between fingers. An array picks one card or a stack, and one deployed system uses a single small cup for single tablets.

tasks.title: Clean high-rise windows
tasks.why: The job is constant-pressure wiping over flat glass, so a force-controlled brush head is the whole effector, as one deployed system shows. Grippers add nothing.

tasks.title: Assemble meal trays on a production line

subtasks.object: a portion from a hotel pan
portion into a moving tray compartment

subtasks.note: Pieces include patties and other items.

tools: Piece-pick attachment, tongs or soft fingers

tasks.why: Portions are bulk materials, so the effector is a scoop sized per ingredient and portion, and discrete items need a grasping attachment. A leading supplier changes utensils per run rather than using one universal hand.

tasks.title: Plate and streak microbiology specimens on Petri dishes

subtasks.object: agar dish from stack and lift lid

subtasks.note: Uses a loop.

subtasks.object: dish, then label and stack it

tools: Parallel gripper for dish base and lid

tasks.why: Dish and lid moves are ordinary rigid picks, while streaking is a light, controlled-contact path that needs a loop. One deployed system uses two robots, but a single arm can switch tools.

tasks.title: Handle vials and syringes for IV compounding

subtasks.object: vial and set it in a holder or on a scale

subtasks.note: This is a fluid step.

subtasks.object: syringe or inject into the bag

tools: Parallel gripper, stepped V-fingers for vials and syringes

tasks.why: The arm only moves rigid containers between fixed stations, and the plunger, needle and scale are stations, not hand tools. One stepped finger set likely holds both vial necks and syringe barrels.

tasks.title: Place raw protein into thermoformed trays

subtasks.object: the piece flat into a tray pocket

subtasks.note: The work runs under washdown hygiene.

tools: Food-grade soft fingers, IP69K washdown rated

tasks.why: Raw meat is wet and limp, so suction leaks and rigid jaws tear it. Soft fingers rated for IP69K washdown meet the hygiene rules and are what deployed lines use.

tasks.title: Feed towels into a folding machine in a commercial laundry

subtasks.object: one towel from the pile by a seam

subtasks.note: Grip both corners once found.
Spread it flat, then feed it in.

tools: Pinch gripper, one per arm on two arms

tasks.why: Narrow pinch jaws grip cloth at a seam or corner. Spreading needs two separate grip points, which one deployed cell gets from rail clamps, with no suction or hand.

tasks.title: Attach milking cups to a cow

subtasks.note: Clean each teat once located.
Spray the teats after removal.

tasks.why: Milking robots carry the cups on the arm and attach them directly. A generic gripper picking cups one by one would be slower and drop cups when a cow kicks.

tasks.title: Fold laundry

subtasks.object: the garment flat by its corners

tools: Parallel pinch gripper, one per arm on two arms

tasks.why: Folding needs two separate grip points and fast regrasping. Two arms with narrow pinch jaws match published systems, though this choice is an estimate.

tasks.title: Scan shelves for out-of-stocks and price errors

subtasks.object: gaps, misplaced items and price errors

tasks.why: Shelf scanning is perception only, so there is no end effector to choose. Telling the user this is itself a useful answer.

rules.title: Single effector on a 6-axis arm by default
rules.text: Always rank first the best single-effector setup on a 6-axis arm with no tool changer. Pick something more complex only if the baseline fails a step outright or the complex setup clearly beats its completion rate for each added effector, and always show the baseline beside it.

rules.title: Six-axis wrist for steps that need tilt
rules.text: When a step opens hinged parts or doors, pours, flips, approaches from the side or below, or processes a non-horizontal surface, compare all effectors on the same 6-axis arm. On a 4-axis top-down wrist, mark the step kinematics-limited and do not rank effectors on it.

rules.title: Use the existing gripper for lids and doors
rules.text: For opening lids, drawers or doors and for pressing, use the gripper already chosen. Move the tool along the hinge arc or push with closed fingers or a held hook or pusher. Soft arms and dexterous hands qualify only if every rigid option fails on a 6-axis arm.

rules.title: Parallel gripper first for rigid parts
rules.text: When a rigid part fits the gripper stroke and its weight under acceleration stays within grip capacity, pick a two-finger parallel or adaptive gripper with form-fit fingertips. Choose pneumatic for a fixed part family with air supply, electric when stroke or force must change.

rules.title: Process steps need dedicated process tools
rules.text: For screwing, nut running, dispensing, painting, sanding, deburring or cutting, require a flange-mounted tool of that kind. A gripper holding a hand tool is allowed only for light, low-torque work and is flagged as improvised.

rules.title: Suction for smooth, flat, sealed faces
rules.text: When a part has a smooth, non-porous flat face large enough for the cups and vacuum force covers the load with a safety factor, pick suction cups. Use flat cups for side loads and stiffness, bellows cups for height variation, curves, cardboard and bags.

rules.title: Tool changer only when tool kinds differ
rules.text: Add an automatic tool changer only when effectors differ in kind or utilities, or cannot share one head within payload, and change time still fits the cycle. Cost each change in seconds plus changer mass. Use manual changers only for batch changeover, never within a cycle.

rules.title: Dual head when two effectors work every cycle
rules.text: When two effectors are used in every cycle and their combined mass with the part fits the payload without interference, pick a dual gripper or multi-function head. Switch by turning the wrist, for example unloading and loading a machine in one visit.

rules.title: Soft grippers only for delicate, light items
rules.text: Soft arms and grippers qualify only for fragile, food or irregular parts of low mass, with no step needing precise placement or applied force such as inserting, screwing, pressing or opening. Otherwise rank them below every rigid option.

rules.title: Dexterous hand as a last resort
rules.text: A dexterous hand qualifies only when a step needs in-hand reorientation or use of a human tool that a gripper, wrist and fixture cannot manage. Apply the largest complexity penalty and show its high price band.

rules.title: Compliance for tight insertions
rules.text: When insertion clearance is smaller than the expected position error, use chamfers with passive remote-centre compliance centred near the tip, or a force-torque guarded search. Do not use a softer gripper in place of compliance.

rules.title: Payload and moment budget
rules.text: Always check that tool, changer and part mass together stay within the arm payload with a dynamic margin. Also check the static moment of the heaviest tool on the changer.

rules.title: Porous faces need high flow or needles
rules.text: For porous faces such as uncoated corrugated cardboard, textile, foam or felt, pick a foam area gripper with a high-flow generator, a needle gripper or fingers. Do not use a small cup on a low-flow integrated pump. For cardboard, use low vacuum and high flow.

rules.title: Magnetic gripper for flat ferrous parts
rules.text: For ferrous parts with a flat face at or above the tool's minimum thickness, pick a magnetic gripper. Derate perpendicular loads to about 28% and cylinders to about 41% of the flat rating, and note that any coating or air gap cuts force sharply.

rules.title: Keep screw reaction torque off the wrist
rules.text: When a screw or nut step exceeds the tool's torque, or reaches 25 N m on a cobot, use a torque reaction arm or a low-reaction tool so the wrist carries no reaction. Screwdriver-class tools stop at about 5 N m.

rules.title: Change fingers before changing tools
rules.text: When every handling step needs the same gripper kind but part families differ in size or shape, pick multi-part fingertips, an adaptive gripper or automatic finger exchange before a full tool changer. This saves cycle time and cell space.

rules.title: Let the gripper hold passive tools
rules.text: When a hook, push, press, scrape or wipe step occurs in a task served by a two-finger gripper, let the gripper pick a passive tool from a holder. No tool changer or extra powered effector is needed.

rules.title: Pneumatic or electric gripper
rules.text: Pick pneumatic when the cell has air, the part family is fixed and the rate is high, for speed, force per gram and cost. Pick electric for high mix, no air or force-sensitive parts, for programmable stroke, speed and force with feedback.

rules.title: Size the stroke and choose the jaw style
rules.text: Choose a stroke just above the largest grasp width, since pneumatic jaws travel the full stroke. Use angular jaws when they must swing clear of the part or machine, and three-jaw centric grippers for round parts.

rules.title: Suction first in bins and clutter
rules.text: When picking from a bin or clutter and items show flat faces, try suction first with fingers as the fallback. Use a hybrid head if both are needed every cycle, as in rule R08.

rules.title: Score process steps by their outcome
rules.text: Score paint, dispense, sand, deburr, screw and insert steps by outcome: coverage and film thickness, path error and steady tool speed, even removal depth, seating at target torque without cross-thread, insert depth under a force limit. Label them approximation tier.

rules.title: Approximation-tier winners need a larger margin
rules.text: When the top setup wins with a soft, suction or process-model effector, show the best rigid-tier setup beside it. Recommend the approximation-tier setup only if it wins by more than the simplicity margin.

rules.title: Separate tools with clashing utilities
rules.text: When two tools need incompatible utilities, such as weld power and gas with vacuum, or paint lines with an electric gripper, or together exceed payload, put them on a tool changer or on separate robots rather than one combined head.
